finding: §4.1.3 says an unimplemented claim "MUST block convergence per §10.2.3", but §10.2.3 reads "Every claim is either mapped to a unit or has an open unimplemented-claim record" — the presence of the entry SATISFIES the condition rather than blocking it, so the cross-reference asserts the opposite of what the target says. The wording is also unsatisfiable after this round's deletion of unanchored records: §4.1.3 states the entry "MUST NOT become a record in `findings.ndjson`" and is instead "recorded in `coverage.ndjson`", while §1.1 defines Open as "Any record in a non-terminal state per §9.1" — a coverage entry has no §9.1 state, so an "open unimplemented-claim record" can never exist. An implementer cannot decide whether an unimplemented claim blocks convergence or permits it.
suggestion: Rewrite §10.2.3 as a blocking condition over coverage state, e.g. "Every claim is mapped to at least one unit, or its unimplemented-claim entry in `coverage.ndjson` has been closed by a note per §3.6 or by a new `cr claims record`", and drop the word `record` so it no longer implies a `findings.ndjson` entry with a §9.1 state.

finding: An unimplemented claim satisfies the convergence condition that §4.1.3 says it must block. §4.1.3 states that an unimplemented-claim entry 'MUST block convergence per §10.2.3' and, in the same breath, that 'It MUST NOT become a record in `findings.ndjson`'. §10.2.3 reads: 'Every claim is either mapped to a unit or has an open unimplemented-claim record.' Read literally, the existence of the entry satisfies condition 3 rather than blocking it, so a pull request that provably implements none of its stated requirements converges. Two further problems make the clause unusable as a test: it calls the thing a 'record' when §4.1.3 forbids it from being one, and it calls it 'open' when §1.1 defines Open as 'Any record in a non-terminal state per §9.1' and a coverage entry has no §9.1 state. Since §4.5.4 and §10.2's closing paragraph make honest reporting of what did not run the point of this section, a converged verdict issued over an unimplemented requirement is the section failing at its own purpose.
suggestion: Rewrite §10.2.3 as a blocking condition over coverage entries, not records: 'Every claim is mapped to at least one unit. A claim with an unimplemented-claim entry in `coverage.ndjson` that has not been closed by a note per §3.6 blocks convergence.' Define the closure mechanism and the entry's lifecycle in §4.1.3, since §9.1 does not cover it.

finding: §10.2.2 requires that 'A unit unchanged since an earlier round keeps its cells' and that each cell 'was filled for that unit's current unit hash per §3.4.6', but §3.4.6 enumerates what a unit records — 'its file paths, hunk ranges, changed line count, a normalised hash of its changed lines called the unit hash, and whether it was formed by symbol, by adjacency, or by fallback' — and never mentions an id, while §6.1 makes `unit` ('The unit id') a required field on every record and §4.5.5 binds every cell to a unit. Nothing says whether the unit id is the unit hash, an ordinal in `units.ndjson`, or something else, and nothing says how last round's cells are matched to this round's units when re-clustering merges or splits them (§3.4.4 and §3.4.5 both re-run every round). The delta-round behaviour §10.2.2 was written to enable is therefore untestable.
suggestion: Define the unit id and its stability rule in §3.4.6, and state that carry-forward matches a prior cell to a current unit on (unit id, unit hash) with any unmatched unit needing a fresh row.

finding: §4.1.3 says an unimplemented-claim entry 'MUST block convergence per §10.2.3', but §10.2.3 states convergence holds when 'Every claim is either mapped to a unit or has an open unimplemented-claim record' — under that wording the entry SATISFIES the condition instead of blocking it, so a PR with every claim unimplemented converges. §10.2.3 also calls the entry a 'record' that is 'open', although §4.1.3 forbids it from becoming 'a record in `findings.ndjson`' and §1.1 defines Open as 'Any record in a non-terminal state per §9.1' — a state machine coverage entries never enter. Condition 3 as written is both inverted and not evaluable.
suggestion: Reword condition 3 to 'Every claim is mapped to at least one unit', and state where an unimplemented-claim entry's resolution is recorded (e.g. a note per §3.6 closing it) so it has an observable open/closed status.

finding: The `cited` row of §6.2 grants `origin: rule` a blanket exemption: a citation qualifies when it "either has `origin: rule` or lies outside the record's own unit". §2.6.1.3 then says a detector hit "MUST be recorded as a `citations` entry per §6.1 carrying the matched `path`, `line`, and `origin: rule`". But `citations` is an agent-written field (§6.1.4 marks only `grade`, `span_hash` and `issue_hash` as computed), and §6.2.3's validation is limited to existence: cr "MUST resolve every entry in `citations` against the current head, and MUST reject ... an entry whose path does not exist or whose line is out of range." No clause requires cr to check an `origin: rule` entry against its own detection output. The result is a self-grading path: any record can attach a citation to its own anchor line, stamp `origin: rule`, and be upgraded from `argued` to `cited` — which §7.2's marker table then allows to be flipped from `question` back to `finding`. This is the one exemption in the grading rules that removes the outside-the-unit requirement, and it is exactly the clause an agent controls.
suggestion: Require cr to write `origin: rule` itself: `cr rules check` records its hits in per-PR state, and at record time cr MUST reject any citation the agent submitted with `origin: rule` that does not match a hit cr produced for that rule, path and line at the current head. Also state that an `origin: rule` citation may support `cited` only when the record carries the matching `rule` id.

finding: §3.7 declares 'cr brief <pr> is read-only. It performs no network write, creates no record', yet requires it to print 'The units of §3.4 with their file paths, hunk ranges, and unit hashes'. No command in §11 is specified to produce `units.ndjson`: `cr review` emits prompts, `cr claims record` stores claims, `cr record` is 'Record a round's merged findings'. `coverage.ndjson` has the same problem — §4.6.3 says 'cr review MUST NOT write to findings.ndjson. It MUST report the set of cells it expects to be filled', and §4.5.5 and §4.1.5 require cells carrying a verdict, a head, a unit hash, an `na` reason and a cited note id, none of which any command accepts as input. Both files are load-bearing for §10.1 and §10.2 yet have no writer, so a test cannot arrange the state under test.
suggestion: Name the command that clusters and persists units (and whether it is idempotent per head), and add an explicit ingestion path for coverage cells — e.g. `cr coverage record <pr> <file.ndjson>` — to §11 and §2.3.

finding: Coverage cells are the substrate of P6 and of §10.2.2 convergence, and several clauses require agent judgement to land in them — §4.4.1 "the classification MUST be recorded in the coverage cell together with the test paths it rested on", §4.1.5 "the coverage cell MUST cite the note id", §4.5.5 "Every cell MUST carry one of `pass`, `finding`, `question`, or `na`" — but no command in §11 writes `coverage.ndjson`. The new §4.6.3 closes the last plausible door: "`cr review` MUST NOT write to `findings.ndjson`. It MUST report the set of cells it expects to be filled" — it reports expectations and fills nothing. `cr record` is specified only for "a round's merged findings", and a `pass` or `na` cell is by definition not a finding, so a unit a role cleared has no channel at all.
suggestion: Specify the write path explicitly: either extend `cr record` to accept coverage cells alongside findings (and define the cell NDJSON schema, its required fields, and its validation), or add a `cr coverage record <pr> <file>` command to §11 and reference it from §4.4.1, §4.1.5, and §4.5.5.

finding: §5.1.6 defines cleanliness as tracked-only: 'Clean means that no tracked file differs from HEAD; untracked files are ignored, because `sandbox.copy` and `sandbox.setup` create them by design.' §5.4.2 then places a gap-probe test file that by construction does not exist in HEAD ('An existing file at that path MUST abort with exit code 4') and asserts 'The removal MUST happen even when the run fails or times out, and §5.1.6 catches the case where it did not.' §5.1.6 cannot catch it — the orphan is untracked, so the sandbox still reports clean, §5.1.7's post-run check also passes, and the next gap probe aborts with exit code 4 over a file `cr` itself left behind. The stated safety net for the gap probe does not exist.
suggestion: Extend the §5.1.6 check with an explicit assertion that no file remains under `probe.test_dir` matching the probe-id naming scheme, or record placed artifact paths in state and verify their absence before every run.

finding: Rung 2 reads 'a run whose executed test count cannot be determined, because the profile declares no `tests.count_pattern`, MUST be `inconclusive`'. The subordinate clause names one cause, but the count is equally undeterminable when `tests.count_pattern` IS configured and simply does not match the runner output. Read as a definition, that case is `inconclusive`; read as an explanation of a narrower condition, the run falls through to rung 3, becomes `no-test-failed`, and §5.3.5 then lets it support a `probed` grade — precisely the outcome §5.3.5 declares impossible ('so neither an over-narrow filter nor an unparseable runner can manufacture evidence').
suggestion: Restate rung 2 condition-first: 'otherwise a run whose executed test count cannot be determined — no `tests.count_pattern` is declared, or the declared pattern did not match the output — MUST be `inconclusive`'.

finding: Rung 3 of §5.3.4 is 'a run in which no test failed'. Nothing records how many tests failed: §5.2.1 records 'exit code, duration, the executed test count when `tests.count_pattern` is configured, and the last `tests.output_tail_bytes` of output', and §5.5 carries only `tests_run`. §5.3.5's second precondition has the same hole — 'only when the filtered baseline of §5.2.2 passed' — since `passed` is never defined for a test run either. The reading decides the single most important mutation case: a mutation that breaks compilation exits non-zero with zero tests failing, which is `failed` (gap disproved, finding forbidden by §5.3.6) under an exit-code reading and `no-test-failed` (gap proved, `probed` grade) under a failure-count reading. Two engineers write mutually contradictory tests on the same run.
suggestion: Define the rung in terms of recorded fields — e.g. 'no test failed' means exit code 0 — or add a `failed_count`/`runner_outcome` field to §5.5 and define both the rung and the baseline 'passed' predicate against it.

finding: §5.3.4 opens 'The result MUST be determined by the first matching rule of this ladder, so the cases never compete' and ends with an unconditional rung, 'otherwise the result MUST be `failed`'. Neither `error` nor `timeout` is a rung, yet §5.5's per-kind table lists both as valid `mutation` results, §5.2.3 requires a run exceeding `tests.timeout_seconds` to be 'killed and recorded as `timeout`', and §5.1.7 requires a probe failing the post-run cleanliness check to be 'recorded with result `error`'. A mutation run that times out therefore has two mandated results and no tie-break. The wrong one is dangerous: §5.3.6 says 'A result of `failed` disproves the gap; `cr` MUST record it and the agent MUST NOT raise the finding', so the ladder reading turns an infrastructure failure into a disproof.
suggestion: Make `error` and `timeout` the first two rungs of the ladder ('a run killed for exceeding tests.timeout_seconds MUST be `timeout`; otherwise a run whose post-run cleanliness check failed MUST be `error`; otherwise ...') so the ladder is total over the §5.5 vocabulary.

finding: §5.3.4 was given a precedence ladder this round "so the cases never compete", and §5.3.5 explains why: "`no-tests-selected` and `inconclusive` MUST NOT support a `probed` grade, so neither an over-narrow filter nor an unparseable runner can manufacture evidence." §5.4 received no equivalent. The §5.5 per-kind table lists `no-tests-selected` as a valid gap result, but no clause in §5.4 says when it is produced or what it means, and §5.4.4 attributes meaning to a bare pass — "A passing gap probe means only the test is missing; severity MUST be at most `medium`" — without requiring that the supplied test actually ran. A filter that selects nothing therefore yields a run with no failures, which §5.4 reads as `passed`, and the gap kind has no `inconclusive` value at all, so a profile without `tests.count_pattern` cannot express "count unknown" for a gap probe.
suggestion: Give §5.4 a determination ladder mirroring §5.3.4 — zero executed tests is `no-tests-selected`; an underivable count is `inconclusive` (add it to the gap row of the §5.5 table); no failure is `passed`; otherwise `failed` — and state that `no-tests-selected` and `inconclusive` support neither a `probed` grade nor the severity floor of §5.4.3 and the severity ceiling of §5.4.4.

finding: §5.4.3 says 'The probe MUST be treated as supporting the finding only when the record names the claim id the test asserts'. 'The record' has two candidates and both fail. The probe record of §5.5 has no claim field at all, so under that reading the condition can never be satisfied and no gap probe ever supports a finding. The finding record of §6.1 has `claim`, but reading it makes grading depend on a third input, contradicting §6.2.1: 'The only inputs are `citations` and the referenced probe record, whose `result` and supporting conditions are fixed by §5.3 and §5.4'.
suggestion: Add a `claim` field to the §5.5 probe record, required for a gap probe that is to support a finding, and state in §6.2.1 that the probe record's `claim` is part of the supporting condition.

finding: §5.5's per-kind table gives `gap` the results `passed`, `failed`, `no-tests-selected`, `error`, `timeout`, but §5.4 never says how a gap result is determined. §5.3.4 supplies an explicit first-match ladder for mutation ('The result MUST be determined by the first matching rule of this ladder, so the cases never compete'); §5.4 has no equivalent — only 'A failing gap probe means either the behaviour is wrong or the supplied test is wrong' and 'A passing gap probe means only the test is missing'. Nothing defines when a gap probe is `no-tests-selected`, and `gap` has no `inconclusive` value at all, so a run whose filter selects zero tests, or a profile with no `tests.count_pattern`, is indistinguishable from `passed` — which §5.4.4 reads as 'only the test is missing' and caps severity at medium on evidence that never existed. I would have to invent the whole mapping from runner exit state to gap result.
suggestion: Give §5.4 a ladder mirroring §5.3.4: error, then timeout, then a known-zero executed count is `no-tests-selected`, then an undeterminable count is `inconclusive` (add it to the gap row of §5.5), then failed, then passed — and state that only `passed`/`failed` may inform severity.

finding: §6.4.4 says "Findings matching an active waiver MUST be dropped and counted per §7.4" and §7.4.6 repeats "Waived findings MUST be dropped before drafting and counted in the round summary", but §9.1 defines no `waived` state and no transition out of `draft` for a waiver. A record that was recorded and then waived therefore stays in `draft`, which §9.1.2 makes an open state, and §10.2.4 then blocks convergence forever on any waived record of severity `critical` or `high` — precisely the records a reviewer is most likely to have waived deliberately. §10.3 compounds this by requiring the round summary to count "waived" as a distinct outcome with no state backing it.
suggestion: Add a terminal `waived` state to §9.1 with a `draft` → `waived` transition produced by `cr record`/`cr merge`, list it in §9.1.2's terminal set, and reference it from §6.4.4 and §7.4.6. If waived findings are meant never to be persisted at all, say so explicitly and explain how §10.3's waived count is derived.

finding: §7.4.1 now makes waiver scope follow disposition: 'a waiver written for `wrong` is scoped to the repository, and one written for `not-here` is scoped to the pull request', and §1.6.3 depends on that scoping. But the command that applies waivers takes no PR: `cr merge <files...> -o <out> --repo <owner/repo>`, justified in §6.5.1 as 'The repository is required because §6.4.4 needs its waivers'. With only `--repo`, §6.4.4 cannot resolve which PR's `not-here` waivers apply. Storage is missing too: §2.2 lists only `~/.cr/waivers/<owner>/<repo>.ndjson`, labelled 'Repository-wide waivers (§7.4)', and §2.3's per-PR table has no waivers file — so a PR-scoped waiver has nowhere to live and no reader.
suggestion: Add a `<pr>` (or `--pr`) argument to `cr merge`, and add a per-PR waivers file to §2.3 so the two scopes have two homes.

finding: The marker table says '`grade` | Immutable; `cr` recomputes it and aborts on a mismatch', while §7.2.2 requires `cr post` to 'recompute every record's grade and re-apply §6.3 before building the payload', and §9.2.5 requires a record whose citation stopped resolving to be re-graded, 'which may demote it to `argued` and therefore to a question'. A legitimate demotion between draft and post produces exactly the mismatch the marker rule aborts on, so §7.2.2's re-application of §6.3 can never fire on a changed grade and §6.3.1's third forcing 'again at post time immediately before the payload is built' is unreachable. `cr` also cannot tell a user edit of the grade field from its own recomputation: §7.1.5 stores only 'every body exactly as rendered' plus a whole-file hash in `rendered.json`, not the marker fields.
suggestion: Abort only when the marker's grade differs from the grade stored in `findings.ndjson` (a user edit); when the recomputed grade differs from the stored grade, re-grade, re-apply §6.3, and report the demotion. Also store marker fields in `rendered.json` so edits are detectable.

finding: §7.3.1 attaches triage events to command invocations rather than to a record-round pair, so the statistics are neither idempotent nor bounded, and the specific honesty MUST of §7.3.4 is falsifiable. Three concrete paths. (a) §8.5.1 defines a full `cr post` run without `--confirm` that validates and prints the payload; §7.3.1 says '`cr post` MUST append exactly one outcome event per queued record' with no `--confirm` qualification, so the dry run the spec's own gate design encourages appends a complete set of outcome events, and the subsequent confirmed run appends them again — double-counting `softened` and `discarded-wrong`, both numerator terms in §7.3.3. (b) §7.1.6 makes the draft regenerable and §7.3.1 says '`cr draft` MUST append one `raised` event for every record it queues', so each regeneration re-inflates the denominator. (c) §9.1's transition table permits `queued` → `discarded` via `cr draft`, but §7.3.1 assigns outcome events only to `cr post`, so a record discarded during draft regeneration is counted as raised and never as discarded. Paths (a) and (b) push the rate in opposite directions depending on workflow, which means §7.3.4's 'cr MUST report it as a lower bound' cannot be honoured: an inflated rate is not a lower bound on anything.
suggestion: Scope triage events to `(record id, round)` and require them to be idempotent: at most one `raised` and at most one outcome event per record per round, with a later emission replacing an earlier one rather than appending. State explicitly that a `cr post` run without `--confirm` emits no triage events, and assign the outcome event for a draft-time discard to `cr draft`.

finding: The pull-request-scoped `not-here` waiver introduced this round has no storage location, no listing command, and no removal command, so the cheapest and most reflexive triage action in the spec is irreversible. §7.2's table makes plain block deletion write a PR-scoped waiver; §7.1.6 states that 'Regeneration MUST NOT resurrect a deleted block'; §7.4.6 drops waived findings before drafting; §9.3.5 carries waivers into every subsequent round. But §2.2's state layout names only `~/.cr/waivers/<owner>/<repo>.ndjson`, labelled 'Repository-wide waivers', and §2.3's per-PR table has no waivers file — the PR-scoped waiver has no home. §7.4.7 offers only `cr waivers list --repo <owner/repo>` and `cr waivers remove <id> --repo <owner/repo>`, both repository-scoped, so a waiver written by a stray keystroke can be neither seen nor undone. This also makes §1.6.3 overstate: 'Triaging to fit under the cap MUST NOT be destructive' is true only repository-wide. Within the pull request, where the review is still running, deleting a true finding for volume reasons in round 1 silences it permanently — including in round 4, when the volume pressure that justified the deletion is gone and §7.4.2's 'stops suppressing once that code changes' does not fire because the author never touched those lines.
suggestion: Give PR-scoped waivers a file in §2.3's per-PR state table, add `--pr <n>` to both `cr waivers list` and `cr waivers remove` in §7.4.7 and §11, and either bound `not-here` waivers to the round that wrote them or require §10.1 to report every active `not-here` waiver each round. Soften §1.6.3 to state the scope of the non-destructiveness it claims.

finding: A `cited` finding is posted to the author as a flat assertion with its evidence withheld. §6.2.4 concedes that record-time validation establishes only that a citation exists, never that it supports the summary. §6.2.5 answers this by requiring every citation of a `cited` record to be rendered verbatim — but only 'into the draft block', which only the reviewer sees. §8.1.4's label, which names the register and the grade, is required only for `kind=question` comments, so a `cited` finding carries neither label nor grade. §8.1.6 establishes the author-facing disclosure principle for exactly two cases — `suggestion_origin: rule` and `source: note` — and does not extend it to citations. The net effect: the author receives 'X is wrong' in Turkish prose, with no location for the basis and no signal that cr checked only that the location exists. This is the spec's most direct remaining path from an unproven claim to a colleague's pull request, and it is the same asymmetry §8.1.6 was added in this round to close.
suggestion: Extend §8.1.6 to citations: every posted `cited` comment MUST name its citations as `path:line` in the body, and MUST state in cr-owned, non-configurable text that cr resolved the location but did not judge that it supports the claim. Alternatively extend §8.1.4's label to every posted comment regardless of `kind`, so the grade always reaches the reader.

finding: §8.3.1 requires that "All comments in a round MUST be posted as one GitHub review, so the author receives a single notification", and §8.4.1 rests the whole partial-failure design on "The GitHub review-creation call is atomic: it either creates the review with all its comments or creates nothing." The reply record introduced this round breaks both: §9.4.2 says the reply is "rendered into the next draft as an ordinary block per §7.1 and posted as a reply inside that thread rather than as a new comment". A reply into an existing review thread is a separate GitHub call from review creation and cannot be an element of the new review's comment array, so a round containing both new comments and replies needs at least two network writes. §8.4 specifies no ordering, no atomicity, and no `post-unresolved` handling for the reply half, and §8.4.3's payload hash is embedded "in the review's own body", which a standalone reply does not have — so §8.4.4's `--reconcile` cannot recognise replies that landed.
suggestion: State in §8.3 that a round's payload has two parts — the review creation and the thread replies of §9.4.2 — fix their order, and extend §8.4 to cover a failure between them: which part is retried, how `--reconcile` identifies an already-posted reply (e.g. by embedding the payload hash in each reply body too), and whether the single-notification promise of §8.3.1 survives.

finding: §8.3.1 requires that 'All comments in a round MUST be posted as one GitHub review, so the author receives a single notification', and §8.4.1 asserts 'The GitHub review-creation call is atomic: it either creates the review with all its comments or creates nothing'. §9.4.2 requires the `partial` reply record to be 'rendered into the next draft as an ordinary block per §7.1 and posted as a reply inside that thread rather than as a new comment'. A reply into an existing thread is not expressible as a comment of a newly created review — the review-creation payload addresses path/line/side, not an existing comment id — so a round containing a reply record needs a second, separate network call. That call is outside §8.4.1's atomicity, outside the single payload of §8.3.3, and outside the embedded payload hash §8.4.4 reconciles against, so a crash between the two calls leaves a state §8.4.4 cannot repair.
suggestion: State explicitly that a round may issue one review-creation call plus N reply calls, define the ordering and what happens when a reply call fails after the review succeeded, and extend §8.3.3/§8.4.4 to cover reply calls.

finding: §8.3.3 requires 'The exact posted payload and its normalised hash MUST be written to `rounds/<n>/posted.json` before the network call', while §8.4.3 requires cr to 'embed the payload hash as an HTML comment in the review's own body before posting'. The review body is part of the payload, so the hash must be computed over bytes that contain it. Either the stored hash is not the hash of the posted payload, or it is unconstructable. §8.4.4's recovery path depends on the answer — it must 'match the embedded payload hash of §8.4.3' against the stored one — so the reconcile test cannot be written until the hashed domain is pinned.
suggestion: Define the payload hash over a canonical projection that excludes the review body (e.g. the ordered comment array with path, line, side and body), and say §8.3.3 and §8.4.3 both use that projection.

finding: §8.4.3 requires `cr` to 'embed the payload hash as an HTML comment in the review's own body before posting', while §8.3.3 requires 'The exact posted payload and its normalised hash' to be written to `rounds/<n>/posted.json` before the call. The review body is part of the posted payload, so the hash would be computed over content that contains the hash. Either it cannot be computed, or the stored hash and the embedded hash are two different values — and §8.4.4's '`cr post <pr> --reconcile` MUST list the PR's reviews, match the embedded payload hash of §8.4.3' does not say which one it is matching.
suggestion: Define the payload hash over a canonical serialisation that excludes the review body (comments array plus PR, head, and round), and state that `posted.json` stores that same hash so the embedded and stored values are identical by construction.

finding: §8.5.4's draft-changed signal is constant-true by construction and therefore implies human involvement it cannot establish — the exact failure §8.5.4 exists to prevent. §8.5.4 says cr can establish only that `--confirm` was given, and that the round summary MUST record that much 'plus the payload hash and whether `draft.md` changed between render and confirmation per §7.1.5'. §7.1.5 calls that hash comparison 'the only observable basis for detecting a user edit'. But §8.1.2 makes an agent edit of every block mandatory: cr renders the initial body in English, then 'the agent then rewrites that body in `render.lang` by editing `draft.md` before the human reads it', and §8.1.1 defaults `render.lang` to `tr`. So under the default configuration the draft file always differs between render and confirmation, always because of the agent, never as evidence of the human. §10.3 then records this signal in every round summary, where a reader of the audit trail naturally reads 'draft changed: true' as the human having touched it. The one positive fact §8.5.4 offers alongside `--confirm` carries zero information about the human and misleads in the direction §8.5.4 forbids.
suggestion: Either drop the draft-changed signal from §8.5.4 and §10.3, leaving `--confirm` and the payload hash as the only things cr claims; or define a second checkpoint hash taken after the agent's §8.1.2 rewrite and immediately before the draft is handed to the human, and record the change only against that hash. Whichever is chosen, §7.1.5 must stop calling the render-time hash a basis for detecting a *user* edit.

finding: The transition table names `cr merge` as a producer: "`draft` | `duplicate`, `suppressed` | `cr merge`, `cr record`", and §9.1.1 requires "Transitions MUST be recorded in `transitions.ndjson`", which §2.3 places under the per-PR state directory. But `cr merge`'s signature in §6.5.1 and §11 is `cr merge <files...> -o <out> --repo <owner/repo>` — it takes no PR, and §6.5.1 justifies the flag it does take purely by waivers and role corpus. `cr merge` therefore cannot locate `~/.cr/state/<owner>/<repo>/pr-<n>/transitions.ndjson`, and the records it dedups do not yet exist in per-PR state (they are files on disk until `cr record <pr> <file>` runs). §11's closing line "Record ids are scoped to a PR, so every command naming one takes the PR" makes the omission deliberate, which makes the contradiction sharper, not softer.
suggestion: Remove `cr merge` from the transition-producer column and state that dedup/suppression decisions travel in the merged file as `state` plus `duplicate_of`/`suppressed_by`, with `cr record` performing and logging the actual `draft`→`duplicate`/`suppressed` transitions. Alternatively give `cr merge` a `<pr>` argument in §6.5.1 and §11.

finding: `regressed` appears in the transition table only as a destination ("`verifying` | `fixed`, `regressed` | `cr verify`") and has no outgoing row, yet §9.1.2 lists the terminal states as "`fixed`, `accepted`, `discarded`, `duplicate`, and `suppressed`. Every other state is open per §1.1." So a regressed record is permanently open, and §10.2.4 — "No open record per §1.1 carries severity `critical` or `high`. This includes records in `regressed` and `stale-anchor`" — makes any high-severity regression an unclearable convergence blocker. §9.6.1 does not help: `cr accept` "MUST apply only to a record in `awaiting-author`, `answered`, or `stale-anchor`". The same reasoning applies to `posted`, which the compound row "`posted`, then `awaiting-author`" leaves without an explicit outgoing transition.
suggestion: Either declare `regressed` terminal in §9.1.2 (the successor record carries the live concern via `regression_of`), or add an outgoing transition — e.g. `regressed` → `accepted` via `cr accept` — and extend §9.6.1's accepted-from list accordingly. Split the `queued` → `posted` → `awaiting-author` row into two explicit rows.

finding: §9.1 states "Transitions are exhaustive. A transition not listed here MUST be rejected with exit code 4", and the only creation row is "— (new record) | `draft` | `cr record`". But §9.4.2 requires `cr verify --outcome partial` to "create a reply record carrying `reply_to`" and §9.4.3 requires that on `regressed` "a new record is created with `regression_of` naming the original". Both are records created by `cr verify`, a command the table never lists as a producer of a new record, so an implementation obeying the exhaustiveness rule must reject with exit 4 exactly the records §9.4 mandates.
suggestion: Add creation rows to the §9.1 table for `cr verify`: "— (new record) | `draft` | `cr verify --outcome partial` (reply record, §9.4.2)" and "— (new record) | `draft` | `cr verify --outcome regressed` (§9.4.3)", and state which state those records enter (`draft` or directly `queued`).

finding: §9.1 states 'Transitions are exhaustive. A transition not listed here MUST be rejected with exit code 4, naming the record and its current state', and the only creation row is '— (new record) | `draft` | `cr record`'. Yet §9.4.2 requires `cr verify --outcome partial` to 'create a reply record carrying `reply_to` ... and `kind: question`', and §9.4.3 requires that on `regressed` 'a new record is created with `regression_of` naming the original'. Both are record creations by `cr verify`, which the exhaustive table must reject. The new records also have no defined starting state, so it is unspecified whether they enter `draft` (and are therefore subject to §6.4 dedup and §7.4 waivers) or go straight to `queued`.
suggestion: Add two creation rows — '— (new record) | `draft` | `cr verify --outcome partial`' and '— (new record) | `draft` | `cr verify --outcome regressed`' — and say whether §6.4 and §7.4 apply to them.

finding: The anchor definition carries 'a normalised content hash of the anchored lines per §1.4' over a range — the anchor has both `start_line` and `line` — but §9.2.2 migrates by scanning 'the new file from line 1 for a line whose normalised hash equals the stored content hash'. For any anchor spanning more than one line, no single line's hash can equal the hash of the multi-line block, so stage 1 yields zero matches by construction. Stage 2's context window is also multi-line, so every multi-line anchor deterministically ends in `stale-anchor` under §9.2.4. One engineer implements the literal single-line scan, another implements a sliding window of (line - start_line + 1) lines; their tests contradict on every multi-line anchor.
suggestion: Say that the scan slides a window of (line - start_line + 1) consecutive lines and compares the normalised hash of the window, and that a single-line anchor is the degenerate case.

finding: The §9.2 preamble defines an anchor as carrying 'path, side, start_line, line, a normalised content hash of the anchored lines per §1.4' — plural, spanning start_line..line. But §9.2.2 migrates by scanning 'the new file from line 1 for a line whose normalised hash equals the stored content hash' — a single-line scan. For any anchor where start_line < line the single-line hash can never equal the multi-line hash, so every multi-line anchor matches zero times at stage one and, absent a rule for the context window at stage two, is forced to `stale-anchor` by §9.2.4 on the first head change. Multi-line anchors are the normal case for records carrying a suggestion, which §8.2.1 defines over 'a contiguous line range'.
suggestion: Restate §9.2.2 as scanning for a window of (line - start_line + 1) consecutive lines whose joint normalised hash equals the stored hash, and say the same for the context-window stage.

finding: §9.2.2 applies migration to "every anchor of an open record", and §9.2.4 requires that an anchor matching zero times or more than once at both stages "MUST move to `stale-anchor`". Per §9.1.2 the open states include `draft`, `queued`, `posted`, `verifying` and `regressed`. But §9.1's exhaustive table permits `stale-anchor` only from "`awaiting-author`, `answered`, `verifying`". A recorded-but-not-yet-posted finding whose anchor dissolves on a push therefore triggers two mutually exclusive MUSTs: §9.2.4 requires the move, §9.1 requires rejection with exit code 4. This is the common case, not an edge case — §9.3 opens a new round on every head change while the previous round's `draft`/`queued` records are still live.
suggestion: Add `draft`, `queued`, `posted` and `regressed` to the from-column of the `stale-anchor` row in §9.1, or scope §9.2.2 explicitly to posted records and state what happens to an unposted record whose anchor no longer resolves (most likely: drop it from the round and count it, since it was never seen by the author).

finding: §9.2.2's second stage says only 'cr MUST scan again for the stored context window, where again exactly one match resolves it', while §9.2.3 requires 'A re-resolved anchor MUST update its line numbers'. The spec never says (a) which line of a matched window becomes the new `line` and `start_line`, (b) whether the anchored line itself is part of the window being matched — if it is, stage 2 can never succeed in the case stage 1 failed because the content changed, making it dead code, (c) how a window with fewer than three context lines at a file boundary is matched, or (d) whether the stored content hash is rewritten after a context resolution, without which every later round repeats the fallback. Every one of these forks produces a different observable line number, which is what a migration test asserts on.
suggestion: Define the stage-2 window as the stored context lines excluding the anchored lines, define the recovered start_line as the line following the leading context block, and state explicitly whether the content hash is refreshed on migration.

finding: The evidence bar for `fixed` is strictly weaker than the bar for `cited`, while §9.4.1 claims it is 'graded like' an assertion. §9.4.1 requires only 'a citation resolving against the new head, or a same-head probe'. §6.2's `cited` row requires more than resolution: the entry must additionally 'either ha[ve] `origin: rule` or lie outside the record's own unit'. §9.4.1 imposes no such qualification, and — more damagingly — does not require the citation to fall inside the author's new changes at all. A citation to any unchanged line of the file resolves against the new head, so 'the author addressed this' can be certified by pointing at code the author never touched. §6.2.4 states plainly that resolution proves existence and nothing more. This matters because `fixed` is not a private bookkeeping state: it is the sole gate to §9.5, whose resolution comment is a network write telling the author their code now addresses the concern.
suggestion: Make §9.4.1's bar at least as strong as §6.2's `cited`, and add the condition that makes it mean what it says: the citation MUST resolve to a line changed between the reviewed head and the new head, or the outcome MUST be recorded as `partial`. State the applicable grade explicitly rather than saying 'graded like one'.

finding: §9.4.1 requires that for the `fixed` outcome 'The record MUST carry a citation resolving against the new head, or a same-head probe; without one the outcome MUST be recorded as `partial` instead', but §11's signature is `cr verify <pr> <id> --outcome <o> --evidence <text>` — free text only, with no channel for a citation or a probe id. Read as 'the record already carries one', the bar is satisfied automatically by the original citations re-resolved per §9.2.5, which point at the code that prompted the finding and evidence nothing about a fix, so `fixed` is granted without evidence and §9.5 resolves the thread on it. Read as 'a citation supplied at verification time', `fixed` is unreachable and §9.5 — 'so `cr verify` and the evidence bar of §9.4.1 remain the only path to `fixed`' — is dead code. Both readings are testable and they disagree completely.
suggestion: Add `--citation <path:line>` and `--probe <id>` to cr verify, and require at least one citation first resolved against the new head (not one carried over from an earlier head) for the fixed outcome.

finding: The resolution comment is a second reader-facing prose channel that §8.1.2 explicitly forbids, and it escapes the entire render contract. §8.1.2 states: 'Editing the draft is the only input path for reader-facing prose: `cr` MUST NOT translate or compose, and MUST NOT accept a body through any other channel.' §9.5.2 then requires that 'The evidence recorded by `cr verify` MUST be carried into the resolution comment, so the author reads why the thread was closed' — text supplied through `cr verify --evidence <text>` (§9.4), never rendered into a draft and never triaged. Three consequences follow. First, §6.1.1 requires `evidence` to be English while §8.1.1 requires posted bodies to be in `render.lang` (default `tr`), so this one posted comment lands in the wrong language. Second, none of §8.1.3, §8.1.4, §8.1.5, or §8.1.6 applies to it, so the provenance disclosures added this round do not reach it. Third, it appears in no `rounds/<n>/posted.json` (§8.3.3 covers only the round payload) and in no §10.3 count, so a posted assertion exists with no entry in the audit trail the spec claims makes 'the history of a review reconstructable from state alone'.
suggestion: Route the resolution comment through the same machinery as any other posted body: render it into the draft as a block, subject it to §8.1.3 through §8.1.6, and record it in `posted.json` and the round summary. If a resolution comment must remain a separate channel, §8.1.2 must name it as the one exception and §8.1 must state which of its rules apply to it.

finding: §9.6 is the one path in the spec where cr admits a posted comment should be taken back, and it is the only such path with no channel to tell the author. §9.6.2 requires evidence 'naming why the concern was withdrawn' and stores it on the record; §9.6.4 forbids resolving the thread; nothing posts a reply. The reviewer's retraction therefore lives entirely inside `~/.cr/` while the original assertion stays open and unanswered on the author's pull request. §9.5.2 grants exactly this courtesy to the `fixed` case — 'so the author reads why the thread was closed' — for the outcome where the reviewer was right; the outcome where the reviewer overreached gets nothing. It is compounded by convergence: §9.6.3 and §9.1.2 make `accepted` terminal, §1.1 defines Open as non-terminal, and §10.2.4 blocks only on open records, so `cr status` can print 'converged' while a comment the reviewer has privately withdrawn is still live in front of the author. Under this spec's own economics, an unretracted wrong assertion left standing is the most expensive state there is.
suggestion: Require `cr accept` to queue a reply record into the next draft carrying the withdrawal evidence — the mechanism §9.4.2 already defines for `partial`, including its §1.6.1 carve-out — so the retraction goes through the ordinary draft, triage, and `--confirm` path. At minimum, forbid a converged verdict while any `accepted` record has an unresolved thread, and surface such records in §10.1.

finding: A normalised hash is 'SHA-256 over the normalised text', but §1.4 defines only per-line transformations and never says how the surviving lines are rejoined or whether the result carries a terminating LF. Step 5's 'Drop leading and trailing blank lines' also never defines blank line, and a text ending in LF splits into a final empty element that one implementer drops as a trailing blank and another keeps. The two readings produce different SHA-256 values for the same input, so no golden-value test can be written for a waiver key (§7.4.1), an `issue_hash` (§3.3), a unit hash (§3.4.6), an anchor content hash (§9.2) or a payload hash (§8.3.3) — despite §1.4's claim that it 'means exactly this transformation and no other'.
suggestion: Add a final step: 'The normalised text is the surviving lines joined by a single U+000A, with no terminating newline', and define blank line as a line that is empty after steps 2-4.

finding: Three per-PR files listed in §2.3 have no command in §11 specified to write them. `units.ndjson` holds the clustering of §3.4, but §3.4 names no command; the only candidate, `cr brief`, is defined in §3.7 as read-only — "It performs no network write, creates no record" — while §4.6.1 and §10.2.2 both consume units as durable state carrying the unit hash of §3.4.6. `threads.ndjson` holds the ingestion of §3.5, which likewise names no command. `coverage.ndjson` is covered separately. Since §2.1.1 requires every command to be "reproducible given the same state directory, the same head SHA, and the same inputs", which command materialises this state and when it is refreshed is load-bearing, not incidental.
suggestion: Name the producing command for each per-PR file in §2.3 or in the owning section — e.g. state that `cr review <pr>` performs §3.4 clustering and §3.5 ingestion and writes `units.ndjson` and `threads.ndjson` before emitting prompts, and that `cr brief` reads them, recomputing in memory when they are absent or stale against the head.

finding: §2.6 item 1 fixes a three-layer resolution order whose lowest layer has no definition anywhere: "Rules MUST resolve in layers, highest first: per-repository, then global, then the profile's built-in rules." §2.2 provides files only for the top two (`~/.cr/repos/<owner>/<repo>/rules/<id>.json` and `~/.cr/rules/<id>.json`); the profile schema in §2.4 declares no field for rules; §2.4.5 pins the two shipped profiles but no rule set; and §11 lists `cr init` as writing "default profiles and roles" with an `--eject-roles` flag but no equivalent for rules. §2.6.3.4's dead-rule pruning and §2.6.1's detection both operate over the resolved corpus, so an implementer must decide unaided whether built-in rules are compiled into the binary, carried in the profile JSON, or written by `cr init`.
suggestion: Either add a `rules` array (or `rules_dir`) to the §2.4 profile field table and say built-in rules travel with the profile, or state that built-in rules are compiled into the binary keyed by profile id and add `cr init --eject-rules` to §11 alongside `--eject-roles`. Either way, say which rules v0.1 ships, as §2.4.5 and §2.5.1 do for profiles and roles.

finding: §2.6 item 1 says 'Rules MUST resolve in layers, highest first: per-repository, then global, then the profile's built-in rules.' Nothing defines that lowest layer: §2.4's profile field table has no rules field (id, match.files, match.globs, axes, sandbox.*, tests.*, symbols.lang), §2.2 lists no path for profile-owned rules, and no section enumerates the built-in rules of the two profiles §2.4.5 requires v0.1 to ship. §2.6.2's `fix` templates and §2.6.1's `detect` blocks therefore have no shipped instance to validate the loader against.
suggestion: Either add a `rules` field to §2.4's profile schema (or a `~/.cr/profiles/<id>/rules/` path in §2.2) and enumerate what `laravel-pest` and `generic` ship, or state that v0.1 ships no built-in rules and drop the third layer from §2.6 item 1.

finding: §2.6.1.5 says 'The agent decides whether a hit is a real violation and MAY dismiss it with a recorded reason', and §2.6.1.6 requires that 'Every hit, record, and dismissal MUST be appended to `rule-stats.ndjson` with the rule id, the round, and the head'. No command in §11 records a dismissal: `cr rules check <pr>` only runs detection, `cr record` writes findings, and no flag carries a dismissal reason. A durable artifact is mandated with no input path — the same defect class §8.1.2 fixed for comment bodies this round.
suggestion: Name the input path: either a `cr rules dismiss <pr> <rule-id> --at <path:line> --reason <text>` command, or a dismissal entry accepted in the merged NDJSON that `cr record` routes to `rule-stats.ndjson`.

finding: §2.7 requires that cr 'MUST reject and report any `CR_`-prefixed variable or config key whose name would address any of them' — the confirmation gate, the argued forcing, and the question label. 'Would address' names no predicate and no list. A tester cannot enumerate the names that must be rejected, so the negative test for invariant 3 cannot be written, and an implementation whose blocklist holds three names is indistinguishable from one holding thirty. It is also unstated whether rejection is exit 1 or exit 3, and whether an unrelated but similarly named key such as CR_CONFIRM_TIMEOUT must be rejected.
suggestion: Enumerate the reserved names as a closed set in §2.7 and require rejection of exactly that set with a named exit code, so the guard has an assertable surface.

finding: §3.3.1 requires cr to 'reject with exit code 1 any claim whose `span` does not occur in the issue text' and §3.3.3 to 'report for each claim whether its `span` still occurs in the new issue text', but neither says whether occurrence is tested on the raw issue text or on the §1.4-normalised text — even though the adjacent `span_hash` and `issue_hash` are both normalised. Since §1.4.4 now collapses interior and leading whitespace, a span copied from a wrapped or re-indented issue passes one reading and is rejected with exit 1 by the other. Accept and reject are the two outcomes a validation test asserts on.
suggestion: State that occurrence is tested by substring match of the normalised span against the normalised issue text, matching how span_hash is computed.

finding: §3.7 introduces `cr brief` as the orientation command and requires it to print six things, only one of which is the issue text. §3.7.2 already anticipates degradation on that one — "with the issue text, or the reason no key was found" — and §3.2 makes the same allowance: "If no key is found, `cr` MUST continue with an empty intent and mark the intent axis unavailable per §4.5." But the failure mode that actually occurs in practice is a reachable key with an unreachable tracker, and §3.1.3 is absolute about it: "A non-zero exit MUST fail with exit code 3 and surface the command's stderr." `cr brief` therefore aborts on a tracker outage or an expired credential, discarding the profile, units, threads, notes and axis report it had already assembled — none of which depend on the tracker. That contradicts the honest-degradation posture of §4.5.4 for a command whose whole purpose is orientation.
suggestion: State in §3.7 (or as a carve-out in §3.1.3) that when `intent.cmd` fails, `cr brief` MUST report the failure and its stderr in place of the issue text, mark the intent axis unavailable per §4.5.3, and still print the remaining items with exit code 0 — reserving exit 3 for commands whose output would be wrong without the intent, such as `cr claims record`.

finding: §4.1.3 requires an unimplemented-claim entry to 'be recorded in `coverage.ndjson` against the intent axis', but §4.5.5's cell shape cannot express it: there is no claim field, the verdict vocabulary is `pass`, `finding`, `question`, `na` — none of which names an unimplemented claim — and the entry belongs to no unit, while §10.2.2 iterates coverage strictly by unit. §2.3.3 additionally requires every record in `coverage.ndjson` to carry a head. There is no defined shape to write, no way to distinguish these entries from ordinary cells when §10.1.2 must report them, and no rule for when an entry stops applying after a later `cr claims record` or a new round.
suggestion: Define a second entry type in `coverage.ndjson` (e.g. `type: unimplemented-claim` with `claim`, `head`, `round`, and a resolution field), and say in §4.1.3 how it is superseded.

finding: §4.3.1 requires candidates 'For every function, method, or class added by the diff', but §4.3.2's qualification is 'A candidate qualifies only when its similarity is at least `reinvention.min_similarity` (default 0.6) and its declared parameter count equals that of the added symbol'. A class has no declared parameter count, so whether a class candidate always qualifies, never qualifies, or is compared on constructor arity is undecidable — three implementations, three test suites. §2.4 also promises no arity data: `symbols.lang` is only a 'Language hint for the reinvention search'. Languages with optional, default or variadic parameters have no defined count either.
suggestion: Define declared parameter count per symbol kind (and for optional/variadic parameters), or restrict the arity filter to functions and methods and state that class candidates qualify on similarity alone.

finding: §4.3.1 requires that when no symbol index can be built 'the reinvention half of this axis MUST be marked unavailable per §4.5 rather than skipped silently'. §4.5 and §10.1.3 model whole axes only — 'Active axes, disabled axes with reasons, and unavailable axes with reasons' — and §4.5.5 gives one verdict per unit-role cell. There is no representation for half an axis, so an implementer must either report the whole `convention` axis unavailable (false: §4.3.5's rule corpus still ran and produced records on that axis) or leave the unavailability invisible, which §4.5.4's 'MUST NOT report a review as complete or converged without stating which axes did not run' forbids in spirit.
suggestion: Introduce a named capability under the convention axis (e.g. `convention.reinvention`) that §4.5 can mark unavailable with a reason and §10.1.3 must print, or split reinvention into its own axis id in §1.5.

finding: §10.2.2 requires 'a complete row of cells for every active role' and §4.6.1 emits prompts 'For every active role of §2.5 and every unit of §3.4', but §4.5.1 defines activity only for an axis: 'An axis is active when it is enabled by the resolved configuration and its prerequisites are met.' No clause defines an active role. §4.6.4 then requires that 'A role whose prerequisites are unmet MUST be reported as skipped, with its reason, never omitted silently' without saying what happens to the cells that role owes, so a run with one skipped role either can never satisfy §10.2.2 or converges on an undeclared exemption. §4.3.1's 'the reinvention half of this axis MUST be marked unavailable per §4.5' has the same gap: §4.5 and §10.1.3 recognise only whole axes, never halves.
suggestion: Define active role (a resolved role whose axis is active and whose `profiles` admits the selected profile), require a skipped role to fill each of its cells with `na` plus the reason, and give the reinvention half an explicit representation rather than reusing axis-level availability.

finding: §4.5.5 enumerates a cell's required fields as 'one of `pass`, `finding`, `question`, or `na`, the head it was filled against, the unit hash of §3.4.6 it was filled for, and a reason when it is `na`' — no unit id, role id, or axis id, although §1.1 defines a cell as 'The intersection of one unit and one active role' and §10.2.2 requires 'a complete row of cells for every active role'. The unit hash cannot stand in for the unit id: §3.4.6 defines it as 'a normalised hash of its changed lines' with no path input, so two units whose changed lines are identical — duplicated boilerplate added to two files — collide, and §10.2.2's per-unit row check silently accepts one unit's cells as the other's.
suggestion: Require `unit`, `role`, and `axis` on every cell, and include the unit's file paths in the unit-hash input so distinct units cannot share a hash.

finding: The review fan-out is the largest cost in the loop and the only expensive mechanism the spec leaves uncapped, while §10.2 makes completing it mandatory. §4.6.1 requires one prompt per active role per unit, each carrying the unit's hunks, its mapped claims, up to `reinvention.max_candidates` symbols, rule hits, test files, threads, and notes; §2.5.5 permits more than one role per axis; §3.4.5 splits any cluster over `cluster.max_lines` (default 80), so unit count grows linearly with diff size and prompt count grows as units × roles with no ceiling. Every other costly mechanism in the spec is bounded and the bound reported when it binds — §1.6.2 `post.max_comments`, §5.6.4 `probe.max_per_round`, §4.4.2 `test.max_edge_cases`, §4.3.2 `reinvention.max_candidates`, §3.4.5 `cluster.max_lines`. §10.2.2 then requires every cell of every unit to be filled for convergence, so the unbounded cost is not optional. §6.4.2's dedup guarantees that the overlap produced by multiple roles on one axis is discarded as duplicates, which is spend that by construction cannot lower the chance of a wrong assertion.
suggestion: Add `review.max_cells` (or an equivalent unit or prompt cap) that, when it binds, blocks with a report naming the unfilled cells rather than silently truncating — the pattern of §1.6.2 and §5.6.4. §10.2.2 should then treat a declared, reported cap the way §4.5.4 treats a disabled axis: convergence may be reported only alongside the statement of what did not run.

finding: §4.6.1 fans out over 'every active role of §2.5 and every unit of §3.4', and §10.2.2 makes convergence depend on 'a complete row of cells for every active role'. But activation is defined only for axes: §4.5.1 says 'An axis is active when it is enabled by the resolved configuration and its prerequisites are met'. §2.5 gives roles a `profiles` filter and §2.5.5 allows several roles per axis, and §4.6.4's 'A role whose prerequisites are unmet MUST be reported as skipped with its reason' never says what a role's prerequisites are or whether a skipped role still owes a cell under §10.2.2.
suggestion: Define 'active role' in §4.5 (axis active, and the role's `profiles` empty or containing the resolved profile), and state whether a skipped role's cells are excluded from §10.2.2's row or filled as `na` with the reason.

finding: §4.6.1 requires `cr review` to emit prompts carrying, among other things, "the rule hits of §4.3.6", and §4.3.6 requires that "A mechanical rule hit MUST be attached to the unit that contains it, so the agent judges an already-located candidate instead of searching for one." But detection is specified in §2.6.1 with no trigger, and §11 exposes it as a separate command, `cr rules check <pr>` — "Run mechanical rule detection over the diff". No clause says `cr review` runs detection, nor that it requires a prior `cr rules check`, nor what it should do when no detection has been run for the current head. A user who follows §13.1's loop — "brief, review fan-out, merge, record, probe, draft, human read, post, recheck" — never runs `cr rules check` at all, so every `detect` rule in the corpus is silently inert.
suggestion: State in §4.6 that `cr review` MUST run §2.6.1 detection for the current head (or MUST fail with a hint naming `cr rules check` when no detection results exist for that head), and add rule detection to the loop listed in §13.1 if it is meant to be a separate step.

finding: §5.3.4 says 'The result MUST be determined by the first matching rule of this ladder, so the cases never compete', and the ladder yields only `no-tests-selected`, `inconclusive`, `no-test-failed`, and `failed`. But §5.2.3 requires a run exceeding `tests.timeout_seconds` to be 'killed and recorded as `timeout`', and §5.1.7 requires a probe whose post-run cleanliness check fails to be 'recorded with result `error`'. Both are valid mutation results in §5.5's table yet unreachable through a ladder that claims to determine the result. Concretely, a timed-out run has no executed test count, so the ladder's second rung labels it `inconclusive`, contradicting §5.2.3.
suggestion: Put `error` and `timeout` at the head of the ladder, above the count-based rungs, so the first-match rule genuinely covers every outcome in §5.5's mutation row.

finding: §5.4.3 ('Severity MUST be at least `high` only when the probe supports the finding') and §5.4.4 ('severity MUST be at most `medium`') name no actor, no enforcement point and no exit code, while §6.1 lists `severity` as an agent-written required field and §7.2's marker table declares `severity` 'Freely editable; recorded as a triage event'. A test cannot decide whether `cr record` rejects a `critical` finding referencing a passing gap probe with exit 1, silently clamps it to `medium`, or accepts it — nor whether the bound is re-applied after a draft edit raises it. The answer is not cosmetic: §10.2.4 blocks convergence on any open record of severity `critical` or `high`.
suggestion: State which command enforces the bounds, whether enforcement is rejection (exit 1) or clamping, and whether §7.2 severity edits are re-checked against the referenced probe at post time.

finding: §5.4.3 makes a claim id the sole gate on a gap probe carrying evidential weight: "The probe MUST be treated as supporting the finding only when the record names the claim id the test asserts; without one the probe MUST NOT support a `probed` grade, which leaves the record `argued` under §6.2 and therefore a question under §6.3." But §6.1 marks `claim` optional — "The claim id, when the axis produces one" — and §4.2.3 explicitly contemplates claimless work: "A unit mapped to zero claims MUST still be evaluated for internal defects." §3.2 goes further: when no issue key resolves, cr "MUST continue with an empty intent", so no claims exist for the whole PR. In that configuration a gap probe can never support a finding no matter what it demonstrates, and since §4.4.4 already forces every unprobed test finding to a question, the test axis loses the ability to assert anything at all — a capability loss that §4.5.4's honesty reporting does not surface, because the test axis is still reported as active.
suggestion: Broaden the anchor of §5.4.3 from a claim id to any recorded assertion target: the claim id when one exists, otherwise the specific behaviour under test named on the record (e.g. a `probe_asserts` field). If the claim requirement is intended, say in §4.5 that the test axis MUST be reported as partially unavailable when the intent axis is unavailable, so the loss is disclosed.

finding: §5.5 defines `baseline` as 'Id of the filtered baseline it was compared against', and §5.3.5 makes a `probed` grade conditional on 'the filtered baseline of §5.2.2 passed'. So a baseline needs an id, a stored pass/fail, and somewhere to live — but the only record type available is the probe record, whose `kind` is constrained to 'mutation or gap' and whose `target` and `input` are both required, none of which a baseline run has. §5.5's per-kind result table likewise has no row for a baseline, so 'the filtered baseline passed' has no vocabulary. §5.2.1 lists what `cr test` records but names no file or id scheme.
suggestion: Either add a `baseline` kind to §5.5 with its own result vocabulary and relaxed required fields, or define a separate `test-runs.ndjson` in §2.3 with an id scheme, and state which stored value §5.3.5 reads as 'passed'.

finding: §5.5's schema marks `baseline` as not required, which contradicts §5.3.5's condition for the only grade that may be posted as a flat high-severity assertion. §5.3.5 states that `no-test-failed` proves the gap 'only when the filtered baseline of §5.2.2 passed', and §5.2.2 requires a filtered probe to record a filtered baseline for the same filter on unmutated code. But the probe record table lists `| baseline | no | Id of the filtered baseline it was compared against |`, and §6.2's `probed` row delegates the supporting condition to §5.3 without naming a field cr can check. A mutation probe recorded with no `baseline` therefore satisfies the schema, and the difference §5.3.5 was written to catch — a genuine test gap versus a filter that selected tests already failing before the mutation — has no mechanical hook. Since `probed` is the one grade §6.3 does not force to a question, an unvalidated `probed` is the shortest path in the spec from a runner artefact to a confident assertion.
suggestion: Make `baseline` required for `kind: mutation` in §5.5's table, and add an explicit clause to §6.2 that a `probed` grade on a mutation probe MUST be rejected with exit code 1 unless the probe names a filtered baseline for the same filter and head whose recorded result was a pass.

finding: §7.1.5 stores 'the normalised hash of the whole draft file. This is the only observable basis for detecting a user edit', and §1.4.4 now collapses 'every run of one or more U+0020 or U+0009 anywhere in a line — including leading indentation — with a single U+0020'. An edit that changes only indentation therefore leaves the hash unchanged and the §8.5.4 draft-changed signal reports false, even though §8.2.3 treats the leading whitespace of a suggestion's first line as significant enough to warn about. Separately, §7.1.6 requires regeneration to 'preserve bodies for records whose body differs from `rendered.json`' without saying whether that per-body comparison is byte-exact or normalised, so one implementation preserves a re-indented body and another silently reverts it.
suggestion: State that the per-body comparison in §7.1.6 and the draft-changed signal of §7.1.5/§8.5.4 are byte-exact, and reserve normalisation for hashing that must survive line-ending differences.

finding: §7.3.1 requires 'cr draft MUST append one `raised` event ... for every record it queues, and cr post MUST append exactly one outcome event per queued record'. Nothing makes either idempotent, and three specified paths break the invariant. §7.1.6 makes the draft regenerable, so a second `cr draft` queues the same records again and appends a second `raised`. §8.5.1's dry run is still a `cr post` ('MUST validate, print the full payload, report "posted": false, and exit 0'), so it appends outcome events that the confirmed run appends again. A `cr post` aborting with exit 1 per §1.6.2 or §8.2.4 leaves `raised` events with no outcome. Worst, §9.1's table lets `cr draft` itself perform `queued`→`discarded` and §7.1.6 says deletions 'become discards and waivers at that moment', so a draft-time discard yields no outcome event at all — structurally violating 'exactly one outcome event per queued record'. §7.3.3's demotion rate is computed from these counts.
suggestion: Key triage events by (pr, round, record id, action) with append-once semantics, require the command that performs a disposition (draft or post) to emit its outcome event, and state that a dry-run post emits none.

finding: §7.3.1 requires that "`cr draft` MUST append one `raised` event ... for every record it queues, and `cr post` MUST append exactly one outcome event per queued record", and §7.3.3 divides by that `raised` count. Two other clauses make both commands repeatable within a round: §7.1.6 states "The draft MUST be regenerable", and §8.5.1 makes `cr post` without `--confirm` a validating dry run that "MUST ... exit 0 without any network call" — an operation a user is expected to run repeatedly while triaging. Nothing scopes the append to a first invocation, so each regeneration adds another `raised` event and each dry run adds another outcome event, inflating the denominator and the numerator of the demotion rate by an amount that varies with how carefully the reviewer worked. §7.3.4 already concedes the rate is a lower bound for a different reason; this adds an unbounded, invisible second distortion.
suggestion: Scope the events by identity: state that at most one `raised` event and one outcome event exist per (record id, round), that regeneration and dry runs MUST NOT append, and that an outcome event is written only by `cr post --confirm` (or by the discard path, for records that are never posted).

finding: §7.3.1 requires that '`cr post` MUST append exactly one outcome event per queued record'. But §8.5.1 makes the ordinary flow two `cr post` invocations: 'without `--confirm` MUST validate, print the full payload, report "posted": false, and exit 0 without any network call', then the confirmed run. Nothing scopes the append to the confirmed run or makes it idempotent, so the documented workflow writes two outcome events per record and every rate in §7.3.3 — including the demotion rate against `stats.demote_threshold` — is computed over doubled denominators. Re-running a dry run several times multiplies the error further.
suggestion: State that outcome events are appended only by a run that passes the gate, or key them on (pr, round, record id) and require the append to be idempotent.

finding: Waiver application is specified at two different stages with no state assigned at either. §6.4.4 says 'Findings matching an active waiver MUST be dropped and counted per §7.4' inside the dedup section applied by `cr merge` (§6.5.1), while §7.4.6 says 'Waived findings MUST be dropped before drafting and counted in the round summary' — which is `cr draft`. §9.1's state list has no waived state and its exhaustive transition table has no waived target, and §6.4.3 deliberately does the opposite for duplicates ('MUST be retained in state `duplicate`'). So it is undefined whether a waived finding ever reaches `findings.ndjson`, and §10.3's mandated 'waived' count has no stated source of truth.
suggestion: Pick one stage, and say whether a waived finding is retained in a `waived` state with the waiver id (consistent with §6.4.3) or discarded at merge and counted only in the merge report that §10.3 consumes.

finding: §8.1.5 makes the presence of one `?` character the whole mechanical guarantee of a question's register, then asserts that this makes the register non-cosmetic: 'The register of a question is not cosmetic: without it, §6.3's forcing changes only a field the reader never sees.' The check is satisfied by a body that asserts flatly throughout and ends with a single tacked-on interrogative, which is the shape agent-composed prose naturally takes when a confident finding has been forced to `kind: question` by §6.3.1. Because §8.1.2 hands body composition to the agent and §8.1.3's only other constraints are non-emptiness and the absence of the marker, nothing prevents the body from contradicting the §8.1.4 label sitting above it. The clause is not wrong, but its justification claims more than the test delivers, and it is the last check standing between a forced `argued` record and an assertion in front of the author.
suggestion: Either weaken §8.1.5's justification to state honestly that the check is a floor and not a guarantee of register, or strengthen the test — for example by requiring the label of §8.1.4 to state in cr-owned text that the item is unproven and that the prose below is the agent's, so the reader's calibration does not depend on the agent's phrasing at all.

finding: §8.1.5 requires cr to 'refuse to post a `kind=question` body containing no `?` character, with exit code 1 naming the record id', while §8.1.4 requires cr to 'prepend a fixed, `cr`-owned label line to every `kind=question` comment'. The term body is used for the draft block text in §8.1.3 ('A body MUST be non-empty and MUST NOT contain the marker comment') and for the assembled comment in §8.1.6 ('Weak provenance MUST be disclosed in the posted body'), so it is unstated whether the check runs before or after the label is prepended. If the built-in label is phrased as a question and the check runs after, §8.1.5 can never fail and the register guarantee it exists to enforce is vacuous.
suggestion: State that the check runs on the record body alone, before the §8.1.4 label is prepended, and that the label is excluded from the test.

finding: §8.2 validates 'A suggestion' and §7.1.3 renders a record's suggestion 'as a fenced `suggestion` block inside the body', but §7.1.2 says 'The block body MUST be free-form Markdown that the user may rewrite entirely' and §7.2 constrains only marker fields. Nothing states whether a fenced suggestion block the user typed into a body becomes the record's `suggestion` and is validated per §8.2 (and what `suggestion_origin` it then carries), or whether it is posted as opaque prose. The two readings differ on the exact observable the section exists to produce: whether a hand-written out-of-hunk suggestion blocks posting with exit code 1 naming the record id.
suggestion: State that cr parses fenced suggestion blocks out of the body at post time, sets suggestion_origin: agent for them, and subjects them to §8.2 — or state that only record-carried suggestions are validated and a body-authored fence is posted verbatim.

finding: §9.2.4 requires an unresolvable anchor to 'move to `stale-anchor` and be surfaced for a decision', but §9.1's exhaustive transition table offers exactly one way out: '`awaiting-author`, `answered`, `stale-anchor` | `accepted` | `cr accept`'. There is no re-anchoring transition, so a still-valid posted concern whose line moved beyond §9.2.2's matcher can only be closed through §9.6, which 'records that the reviewer withdrew a posted concern after discussion' — a statement that is false in this case — while §10.2.4 keeps counting it as blocking convergence. The decision §9.2.4 mandates has no command that implements it.
suggestion: Add a re-anchor transition ('`stale-anchor` | `verifying` or `awaiting-author` | `cr recheck --reanchor <id> --at <path:line>'), re-validated per §9.2, so a stale anchor can be repaired without asserting a withdrawal.

finding: §9.2.2 pins migration to a uniqueness test: "`cr` MUST scan the new file from line 1 for a line whose normalised hash equals the stored content hash; exactly one match resolves the anchor. On zero matches or more than one, `cr` MUST scan again for the stored context window, where again exactly one match resolves it." Combined with §1.4.4, which collapses "every run of one or more U+0020 or U+0009 anywhere in a line — including leading indentation — with a single U+0020", the first pass is indentation-insensitive, so ordinary single-line anchors (`}`, `end`, `return null;`, `});`) will match many times in any real file, and the second pass inherits the same insensitivity for its context window. §9.2.4 then forbids the obvious tie-break — "`cr` MUST NOT choose between candidates" — sending the record to `stale-anchor`, which §10.2.4 makes a convergence blocker. As specified, the common case for short lines is failure, and the failure is unrecoverable except through `cr accept`.
suggestion: Add a deterministic, non-guessing tie-break that does not require cr to judge: among equal-hash candidates prefer the one nearest the stored line number and require the stored context window to match at that position in the first pass rather than only as a fallback. If ties remain, then move to `stale-anchor`. State the anchor width requirement too (e.g. a single-line anchor MUST store its context window).

finding: §2.6 numbers both its subsections (§2.6.1 Detection, §2.6.2 Fixes, §2.6.3 Harvesting) and its own list items 1-5, so a reference of the form §2.6.3 is ambiguous. This round's §2.6.1.3 relies on the ambiguous form: "The rule id is carried separately on the record per §2.6.3." §2.6.3 is the Harvesting subsection, which says nothing about carrying a rule id; the intended target is §2.6 item 3, "Every record produced by a rule MUST carry the rule id." §8.1.6's "per §3.6.3" has the same shape and happens to be correct only because §3.6 has no subsections.
suggestion: Point §2.6.1.3 at the §6.1 `rule` field, which is where the requirement is actually operative, or introduce an unambiguous convention for list items (e.g. "§2.6, item 3") and apply it wherever a section carries both subsections and numbered items.

finding: §2.6.1.1 evaluates a detect block 'over the added and modified `RIGHT`-side lines of the diff only — never over removed lines, and never over the whole repository'. A unified diff distinguishes added lines and context lines on the RIGHT side; there is no 'modified' line a parser can identify. One implementation matches only `+` lines, another matches every RIGHT-side line inside a changed hunk including unchanged context, and a rule-hit count test disagrees between them.
suggestion: Say 'over the added (`+`) lines of the diff only', dropping 'modified', or define modified explicitly in terms of the diff format.

finding: §7.4.1 keys a waiver by '(anchor.path, class, rule id when present, normalised hash of the anchored lines)'. Because one component is conditional the key has two shapes, and the spec never says whether a waiver written without a rule id matches a later record that carries one at the same path, class and hash, or the reverse. A waiver-suppression test has no defined expected result for the mixed case.
suggestion: Make the rule id an always-present key component with an explicit empty value, and state that an empty rule id matches only records with no rule id.
